headline: Andreessen Horowitz's latest ranking of consumer AI apps shows that few people pay for AI, with the top one percent of spenders making up nearly a fifth of the spending it tracked, The Decoder reports.
score_reason: Pool score 5 lowered by 1: a16z published this ranking by 6 Oct 2026 and our 6 Oct edition carried it; The Decoder's 10 Oct write-up adds spending detail but is not a new event.
importance_line: What changed is that card data shows AI income resting on a small group of heavy paying users, which matters first to the free majority who may fall behind in skills, then to investors counting on mass consumer income, then to AI firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and the doubt is that the figures come from a sample of US cards, not total revenue, in a ranking by a firm that invests in the field.
summary: The Decoder reports that the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), in the seventh edition of its Top 100 consumer AI list, which our 6 Oct 2026 edition carried, found that nearly half of US consumers use AI but only 4.5% held a paid personal subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude in August. What The Decoder adds is that the top 1% of spenders, averaging about $900 a month, account for nearly a fifth of the card spending a16z tracked, more than the whole bottom half combined, while the typical payer spends about $25.
notes: Read from the pre-fetched full text. Older news re-dated: our 6 Oct 2026 edition (item 90) carried a16z's own publication of this list. New in The Decoder: the top 1% share, the $900 and $25 figures, and the agent and Muse detail. Its remark that a skills gap could deepen inequality is its own comment, not a finding.
